predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text contains an embedded, self-critical paragraph: 'The residual labels in Equation (2) are ambiguously defined, potentially conflicting with label smoothing interpretations and masking operations. Moreover, summing classification loss for current classifier, all classifiers, and previous classifiers in Equation (5) may double-count errors and create conflicting optimization objectives. The shared encoder update assumption is unaccounted in loss definitions, risking unstable training. Precise formulations for lambda's role and element-wise operations need clarification to ensure mathematical consistency.' This appears to be a reviewer or note left in the manuscript, not part of the final paper. It highlights unresolved ambiguities and possible errors in the method's formulation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A, Lemma 1 proof (Equation 18 and surrounding text)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The proof of Lemma 1 claims that due to strong convexity there exists ρ ∈ (0,1) such that ||Φ(t) - Φ*|| ≤ ρ^t ||Φ(0) - Φ*||. Strong convexity alone does not guarantee linear convergence of the parameter iterates to the optimum; this requires assumptions on the optimization algorithm and learning rate that are neither stated nor justified. The claimed inequality is therefore unjustified, undermining the entire theoretical analysis.

Residual labels are defined as y_i - λ Σ_{j=1}^{t-1} y_i ⊙ p_{ij}^o. The text claims that using y_i to mask non-ground-truth labels ensures non-negativity. However, Σ p_{ij}^o for the ground-truth class can exceed 1, so the expression can become negative for λ > 0 when Σ p > 1/λ. The claim of non-negativity is therefore mathematically incorrect, and the definition is ambiguous regarding label softening.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.3, adaptive classifier assignment score s_t^o = (1/N) Σ_i y_i^⊤ [ Σ_j p_{ij}^o ]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The confidence score is a sum over all classifiers of the predicted probability of the true class, not normalized by the number of classifiers n^o. As more classifiers are added to a modality, its score artificially increases, making the gap s_t^a - σ s_t^v dependent on the current number of classifiers rather than purely on per-classifier performance. This can distort the adaptive assignment logic and is not addressed.

The theoretical analysis assumes a continuous gradient boosting update (Φ(t+1)=Φ(t)+η h(Φ(t))) applied at every step, whereas the actual method adds classifiers only when the confidence gap exceeds a threshold and only every t_N epochs. The theorem's convergence guarantee therefore does not directly apply to the proposed adaptive classifier assignment algorithm, yet the paper presents the theory as a justification for the method's effectiveness.

Reference [10] reads: 'W. et al. What Makes Training Multi-Modal Classification Networks Hard? In CVPR, 2020.' This is a duplicate of reference [40] (Wang et al., same title) but with incomplete authorship ('W. et al.') and missing page numbers. This constitutes a malformed and redundant citation.

The abstract states: 'our method ... outperforming several recent baselines by a modest margin.' The conclusion states: 'our proposed method can achieve state-of-the-art performance compared with various baselines by a large margin.' These are contradictory characterizations of the performance gains.

The paper refers to loss components ϵ, ϵo, ϵp from Equations (2), (3), and (4), but Equations (3) and (4) are never shown in the manuscript. The ablation study in Table 2 uses these symbols without definition, making the experiment impossible to interpret.
